A-level Philosophy · Epistemology

What is knowledge?

How should propositional knowledge be defined? A guided route from Plato’s three conditions, through Gettier’s famous counter-examples, to the theories that try to repair the definition.

Introduction

The question: what is knowledge?

Before we can say what, how or how much anyone knows, we need to agree on what knowledge is. This section of the course looks for a definition.

We use the word “know” constantly: I know the way home, I know Sam, I know that water boils at 100°C. Philosophers notice that these are different kinds of knowing, and that only one of them is the focus of this topic.

Three kinds of knowledge

Propositional knowledge

Knowing that. Knowledge of a state of affairs that can be written as a sentence that is true or false.

“Paris is the capital of France.”

This topic

Acquaintance knowledge

Knowing a person, place or thing through direct contact with it.

“I know Oxford.” “I know John.”

Ability knowledge

Knowing how to do something; a practical skill.

“I know how to ride a bicycle.”

Why propositional knowledge? A proposition is a claim that is either true or false. This makes propositional knowledge the kind we can test most precisely: we can ask whether the claim is true, whether the person believes it, and what reasons they have. Those three questions lead directly to the first definition we will study.

Your route through the topic

★Exam questions

3, 5, 12 and 25-mark questions with planning points.
The whole topic in one line

Is knowledge justified true belief, or must we drop a condition, add one, change one, or give up on defining knowledge altogether?

Part 1

How philosophers define concepts

To define something, philosophers look for its necessary and sufficient conditions: the features that pin down exactly what does and does not count.

When philosophers seek the necessary and sufficient conditions of something, they are looking for its definition. A definition of this kind does more than describe typical examples. It draws a precise boundary: everything inside the boundary counts, and everything outside does not.

Necessary conditions

A necessary condition is something you must have. If it is missing, you cannot have the thing being defined.

The testA is necessary for B if: without A, there is no B.

Example

Being a mammal is necessary for being a dog. If something is not a mammal, it cannot be a dog.

But not enough

Being a mammal is not sufficient for being a dog. A cat is a mammal and is not a dog.

Sufficient conditions

A sufficient condition is something that is enough. If you have it, you definitely have the thing.

The testA is sufficient for B if: whenever there is A, there is B.

Example

Being a dog is sufficient for being a mammal. If something is a dog, it is definitely a mammal.

But not required

Being a dog is not necessary for being a mammal. Whales and humans are mammals too.

Being inside the small circle (dog) is sufficient for being inside the big circle (mammal). Being inside the big circle is necessary for being inside the small one.

Putting them together: “if and only if”

A full definition gives conditions that are individually necessary (each one is required) and jointly sufficient (together they are enough). Philosophers signal this with “iff”, short for “if and only if”.

Water

The necessary and sufficient condition of water is H₂O. When you have hydrogen and oxygen combined in a specific way, you have water. When you have water, you have hydrogen and oxygen combined in that way. The necessary conditions are what you must have; the sufficient conditions are all the things you need.

Bachelor

X is a bachelor iff (1) X is a man and (2) X is unmarried.

  • Each is necessary: a married man is not a bachelor; an unmarried woman is not a bachelor.
  • Together they are sufficient: any unmarried man is a bachelor.

The search for knowledge’s definition

Gettier opens his famous 1963 paper by describing exactly this project:

“Various attempts have been made in recent years to state necessary and sufficient conditions for someone’s knowing a given proposition.”

Edmund Gettier, ‘Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?’ (1963)

So our question becomes: what must be true of a person, S, and a proposition, P, for it to be correct to say “S knows that P”?

Two ways to attack a definition

There are only two ways to show that a proposed definition fails. These two attacks organise the rest of the topic.

Attack 1: “Not necessary”

Find a case where we clearly have the thing, but one of the conditions is missing. That condition was not necessary after all.

See Part 3 →

Attack 2: “Not sufficient”

Find a case where all the conditions are met, but we clearly do not have the thing. The conditions were not enough.

See Part 4 →

Check your understanding

Is “having four legs” necessary, sufficient, both, or neither for being a dog?

Neither. Not necessary: a dog that has lost a leg is still a dog. Not sufficient: a table has four legs and is not a dog.

Is “being a square” necessary or sufficient for “being a rectangle”?

Sufficient, not necessary. Every square is a rectangle, but many rectangles are not squares.

Which kind of counter-example would show that “truth” is not necessary for knowledge?

A case where someone clearly knows something that is not true. (Part 3 looks at whether such cases exist.)

Part 2

The tripartite view: justified true belief

The classic definition says knowledge has three parts. Each is necessary; together they are sufficient.

The tripartite (“three-part”) view is usually traced back to Plato. In the Theaetetus, Plato considers the idea that knowledge needs three ingredients: belief, truth and justification. Gettier himself notes the connection in a footnote:

“Plato seems to be considering some such definition at Theaetetus 201, and perhaps accepting one at Meno 98.”

Edmund Gettier (1963)
The tripartite definition S knows that P if and only if:
  1. P is true;
  2. S believes that P; and
  3. S is justified in believing that P.

S stands for the subject (the knower) and P for the proposition. Gettier states the view in exactly this form in his paper, labelling it definition (a).

Reading the diagram

  • Truth + belief only: a lucky guess.
  • Belief + justification only: a reasonable mistake.
  • Truth + justification only: good evidence for something true that the person does not accept.
  • All three: knowledge, according to the tripartite view.

Why each condition seems necessary

Truth

You cannot know something false. People once believed the Sun travels round the Earth; we say they believed it, not that they knew it. If P is false, the most we can say is that someone thought they knew.

Belief

It sounds contradictory to say “I know Paris is the capital of France, but I don’t believe it.” Knowing seems to involve accepting the claim. Knowledge is something a person has, and belief is the state in which they hold it.

Justification

A lucky guess is not knowledge. If I guess the winning lottery numbers and they come up, I had a true belief, but no reason for it. Justification means having reason or evidence for believing P.

Why they seem jointly sufficient

If you believe P, P is true, and you have good reasons for believing P, it seems there is nothing left to add. To know that Paris is the capital of France, you believe it, you have evidence for it (maps, teachers, visits), and it is true. What more could knowledge require?

Other versions of the same idea

Gettier shows that leading twentieth-century philosophers held their own versions of the three-part view. He quotes them:

“S knows that P IFF (i) S accepts P, (ii) S has adequate evidence for P, and (iii) P is true.”

Roderick Chisholm, Perceiving (1957), quoted by Gettier

“S knows that P IFF (i) P is true, (ii) S is sure that P is true, and (iii) S has the right to be sure that P is true.”

A. J. Ayer, The Problem of Knowledge (1956), quoted by Gettier

Notice the shared structure: a truth condition, a belief condition (“accepts”, “is sure”), and a justification condition (“adequate evidence”, “the right to be sure”). Gettier argues that his counter-examples defeat all three versions.

Two lines of attack

Critics either deny that one of the three conditions is necessary (Part 3), or argue that the three together are not sufficient, so something more is needed (Part 4).

Part 3

Do we really need all three conditions?

Attack 1: if we can find knowledge without one of the conditions, that condition is not necessary, and the tripartite definition is wrong.

Knowledge without justification?Foley
Knowledge without belief?Lottery winner, nervous student
Knowledge without truth?Kuhn, the “flat” table

A · Knowledge without justification

Richard Foley argues that we can drop justification. On his view, knowing is a matter of having a true belief that is not missing anything important.

“To know is to have truth and adequate information.”

Richard Foley, as summarised in the course handout ‘What is knowledge?’

What matters, for Foley, is that a true belief does not lack important information, or leave out some aspect of the situation that bears on whether P is true.

The stopped clock

Someone looks at a clock that stopped working the day before but happens to show the right time: 12 o’clock. They come to believe it is 12, and it is. They do not know the clock has stopped.

Most philosophers say this person lacks proper justification. Foley says instead that they lack important information relevant to the situation: that the clock is no longer working. That missing information, not missing justification, explains why they do not know.

Supporting point

Young children and animals seem to know things (where their food is, who their parent is) without being able to give any reasons. If knowledge required justification in the sense of being able to give reasons, they would know nothing. This point is developed by reliabilism in Part 5.

Objection: prejudice

If true belief (without justification) can be knowledge, we open the door to prejudice. Someone might believe a person is guilty because of the colour of their skin. Even if that person happens to be guilty, this is obviously not knowledge. Justification is exactly what rules out beliefs held for bad reasons.

Response

Foley can reply that the prejudiced person also lacks adequate information: they are missing all the information that actually bears on guilt (evidence, alibis, witnesses). So his condition rules out prejudice too, without needing a separate justification condition.

Counter-response

If “adequate information” rules out exactly the cases that justification rules out, it may simply be justification under a new name. In that case Foley has not shown that knowledge is possible without justification; he has redescribed it.

B · Knowledge without belief

Some philosophers claim there are cases where a person knows something without believing it.

The lottery winner

Someone checks their ticket against the numbers on television. The numbers match. They can spend some time still not believing that they have won, while clearly knowing that they have won.

The nervous student

A student thinks they do not know the answers on a multiple-choice test in a foreign language. Yet they get full marks. They seem to know the answers without believing that they know them.

Response to the lottery winner

“I don’t believe it!” expresses shock, not a genuine absence of belief. If the winner truly did not believe they had won, they would not go and claim the prize. Their actions show the belief is there.

Response to the student

Either the student is guessing, or they are not. If they are guessing, they lack justification, so the tripartite view correctly says this is not knowledge. If they are not guessing, they do believe the answers (they choose them deliberately); what they lack is a belief that they know. The case therefore shows knowledge without confidence, not knowledge without belief.

Counter-response

Defenders of the objection may insist that a state the person sincerely denies cannot really be called belief. The debate then turns on what belief is: a feeling of conviction, or a disposition shown in what we do.

C · Knowledge without truth

The course handout identifies two forms of this argument.

1 · “Truth” with a capital T

This form, associated with Thomas Kuhn, denies that science will ever reach a complete theory of everything. Science keeps progressing and its theories are transformed, so beliefs we now treat as true may not be considered true in future.

Newtonian mechanics was once accepted as correct and is still widely used, yet strictly speaking it is false in the light of Einstein’s theory of relativity. If knowledge needs truth, did physicists before Einstein know nothing about motion?

2 · truth with a small t

This form claims that no ordinary proposition is ever strictly correct.

I claim that the table I am eating lunch on is flat. Under a powerful microscope its surface is uneven, so strictly speaking the claim is false. Yet surely I know the table is flat. So we can have knowledge without strict truth.

Response to form 1

Science may one day reach a complete theory of everything, giving us Truth with a capital T, and with it knowledge. Until then, we can say that earlier scientists had very well-justified beliefs, but not knowledge, wherever their theories were false.

Response to form 2

The claim “the table is flat” is “true enough”. In ordinary contexts, “flat” means flat enough to eat from, and in that sense the claim is simply true. The microscope changes the standard, not the truth of what I said.

Counter-response

If truth depends on context and standards, the truth condition is less straightforward than the tripartite view assumes. A full definition of knowledge would need to say which standard of truth applies.

D · Can knowledge be defined at all?

Timothy Williamson takes a more radical line. He argues that knowledge cannot be analysed, because it is itself a basic concept, and basic concepts cannot be broken down into simpler ones.

On his view, the order of explanation runs the other way: it is because we know things that we have beliefs, evidence and truth, not the reverse. Knowledge is a factive mental state, a state that connects you to the world. Belief is not factive: belief only aims at truth, so it is not necessarily connected to how the world is.

What follows: if Williamson is right, the whole project of Parts 1 to 5 (searching for necessary and sufficient conditions) is mistaken from the start. The repeated failure to find a definition that survives counter-examples could be taken as evidence that he is right.

Part 4

Justified true belief is not enough: Gettier

Attack 2: a three-page paper from 1963 that showed someone can have a justified true belief and still not know.

In 1963 Edmund Gettier published “Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?” in the journal Analysis. Unlike the arguments in Part 3, Gettier does not deny that truth, belief and justification are necessary. He argues that they are not jointly sufficient.

“I shall argue that (a) is false in that the conditions stated therein do not constitute a sufficient condition for the truth of the proposition that S knows that P. The same argument will show that (b) and (c) fail if ‘has adequate evidence for’ or ‘has the right to be sure that’ is substituted for ‘is justified in believing that’ throughout.”

Edmund Gettier (1963)

Here (a) is the tripartite definition, (b) is Chisholm’s version and (c) is Ayer’s (see Part 2).

Gettier’s two starting points

Gettier’s argument rests on two claims that most philosophers accept.

1

Justification is fallible.

“In that sense of ‘justified’ in which S’s being justified in believing P is a necessary condition of S’s knowing that P, it is possible for a person to be justified in believing a proposition that is in fact false.”

Edmund Gettier (1963)
2

Justification carries over through deduction (often called the principle of closure).

“For any proposition P, if S is justified in believing P, and P entails Q, and S deduces Q from P and accepts Q as a result of this deduction, then S is justified in believing Q.”

Edmund Gettier (1963)

Why these matter: point 1 lets Smith be justified in believing something false. Point 2 lets that justification pass from the false belief to a new belief. If the new belief happens to be true, the result is a justified true belief built on a mistake.

Case I: the ten coins

“Suppose that Smith and Jones have applied for a certain job. And suppose that Smith has strong evidence for the following conjunctive proposition: (d) Jones is the man who will get the job, and Jones has ten coins in his pocket. Smith’s evidence for (d) might be that the president of the company assured him that Jones would in the end be selected, and that he, Smith, had counted the coins in Jones’s pocket ten minutes ago. Proposition (d) entails: (e) The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.”

Edmund Gettier (1963), Case I
EvidenceThe company president says Jones will get the job. Smith counted ten coins in Jones’s pocket.
→
(d) Jones will get the job, and Jones has ten coinsFalse: Jones does not get the job
→
(e) The man who will get the job has ten coinsTrue: by luck, because of Smith’s own pocket

“But imagine, further, that unknown to Smith, he himself, not Jones, will get the job. And, also, unknown to Smith, he himself has ten coins in his pocket. Proposition (e) is then true, though proposition (d), from which Smith inferred (e), is false.”

Edmund Gettier (1963), Case I
ConditionMet?Why
Truth✓The man who gets the job (Smith) does have ten coins in his pocket.
Belief✓Smith accepts (e) on the grounds of (d).
Justification✓Smith has strong evidence for (d), and (d) entails (e), so by closure he is justified in believing (e).
Knowledge?✗(e) is true because of Smith’s coins, but Smith’s belief is based on counting Jones’s coins.

“It is equally clear that Smith does not know that (e) is true; for (e) is true in virtue of the number of coins in Smith’s pocket, while Smith does not know how many coins are in Smith’s pocket, and bases his belief in (e) on a count of the coins in Jones’s pocket, whom he falsely believes to be the man who will get the job.”

Edmund Gettier (1963), Case I

Case II: the Ford and Barcelona

“Let us suppose that Smith has strong evidence for the following proposition: (f) Jones owns a Ford. Smith’s evidence might be that Jones has at all times in the past within Smith’s memory owned a car, and always a Ford, and that Jones has just offered Smith a ride while driving a Ford.”

Edmund Gettier (1963), Case II

Smith has another friend, Brown, whose whereabouts he does not know at all. Choosing three place-names “quite at random”, Smith constructs three propositions, each of which is entailed by (f):

(g)

Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Boston.

(h)

Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Barcelona.

(i)

Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Brest-Litovsk.

Because each follows from (f), for which Smith has strong evidence, Smith is justified in believing all three. Then the twist:

“First, Jones does not own a Ford, but is at present driving a rented car. And secondly, by the sheerest coincidence, and entirely unknown to Smith, the place mentioned in proposition (h) happens really to be the place where Brown is.”

Edmund Gettier (1963), Case II

So (h) is true (because Brown is in Barcelona), Smith believes it, and he is justified. Yet Smith “has no idea where Brown is”. He does not know (h).

Gettier’s conclusion

“These two examples show that definition (a) does not state a sufficient condition for someone’s knowing a given proposition. The same cases, with appropriate changes, will suffice to show that neither definition (b) nor definition (c) do so either.”

Edmund Gettier (1963)

More Gettier-style cases

Once the pattern is clear, it is easy to build more examples.

The stopped clock

Someone looks at a stopped clock that happens to show the correct time. They have a justified true belief about the time, but they do not know it.

Henry in Barn County

Henry sees the one real barn in a county full of fake barn façades. His belief is true, but only by luck. This case becomes central in Part 5.

What Gettier shows

Justification can be fallible, so a justified belief can be true by luck. When that happens, we have justified true belief without knowledge. The tripartite definition must be adapted: by adding a condition, replacing one, or abandoning the search for a definition.

Part 5

New definitions of knowledge

Four attempts to repair or replace justified true belief. Each is explained, then evaluated through objections, responses and counter-responses.

TheoryKey thinkersWhat it does to JTBIn short
No false lemmasResponse to GettierAdds a fourth conditionJTB, not inferred from anything false
InfallibilismDescartesStrengthens justification into certaintyTrue belief that cannot be wrong
ReliabilismGoldman (Ramsey, Armstrong)Replaces justification with reliabilityTrue belief from a reliable process
Virtue epistemologySosa, ZagzebskiReplaces justification with intellectual virtueTrue belief that is true because of competence

Infallibilism is the only one of these four that was not formulated as an answer to the Gettier puzzle.

A · No false lemmas (JTB + N)

A lemma is a proposition used as a step in an argument on the way to a conclusion. In both of Gettier’s cases, Smith reaches a true conclusion by way of a false lemma:

Case I false lemma

“Jones is the man who will get the job.”

Case II false lemma

“Jones owns a Ford.”

The proposal: we cannot know a truth by reasoning through a falsehood. So we plug the gap with a fourth condition.

No false lemmas definition S knows that P if and only if:
  1. S believes that P;
  2. P is true;
  3. S is justified in believing that P; and
  4. S has not inferred P from any false proposition.
Strength

It deals neatly with both of Gettier’s original cases. Smith’s beliefs in (e) and (h) were inferred from false propositions, so the fourth condition is not met and Smith does not know. This matches our intuition exactly. It also keeps the familiar structure of the tripartite view and simply adds to it.

Objection: Henry in Barn County

Alvin Goldman (1976), crediting the example to Carl Ginet, describes a case of justified true belief with no false lemma that is still not knowledge:

“Suppose there is a county in the Midwest with the following peculiar feature. The landscape next to the road leading through that county is peppered with barn-facades: structures that from the road look exactly like barns. Observation from any other viewpoint would immediately reveal these structures to be fakes: devices erected for the purpose of fooling unsuspecting motorists into believing in the presence of barns. Suppose Henry is driving along the road that leads through Barn County. Naturally, he will on numerous occasions form false beliefs in the presence of barns. Since Henry has no reason to suspect that he is the victim of organized deception, these beliefs are justified. Now suppose further that, on one of those occasions when he believes there is a barn over there, he happens to be looking at the one and only real barn in the county. This time, his belief is justified and true. But since its truth is the result of luck, it is exceedingly plausible to judge that Henry’s belief is not an instance of knowledge.”

Alvin Goldman (1976)

Henry believes there is a barn; it is true; he is justified; and his belief is a direct perception, not inferred from any false proposition. All four conditions are met, yet he does not know.

Response: a fifth condition

Add a further condition: if you are in a strange situation (like Barn County), you must know that you are. Henry does not know he is in Barn County, so he fails this condition and does not know.

Counter-response: the bar is now too high

We can never know in advance that we are not in a strange situation. Radical scepticism shows this: if you were a brain in a vat being fed a digital simulation of real life, nothing in your experience would reveal it. So the fifth condition can never be satisfied, and we would know almost nothing.

B · Infallibilism

Infallibilism, developed by René Descartes, understands justification in terms of certainty. On this view you are not really justified if you could possibly be wrong; genuine justification guarantees that your belief is true. To know something, you must be certain of it.

Infallibilist definition S knows that P if and only if:
  1. P is true;
  2. S believes that P; and
  3. S’s justification for P makes it impossible for S to be wrong (S is certain).

This can be presented either as replacing justification with certainty, or as clarifying what real justification has always meant.

What does “certain” mean?

(a) Feeling certain

A psychological state of being sure. This cannot be right: people often feel certain and turn out to be wrong, so feeling certain does not guarantee truth.

(b) Rational certainty

A belief that cannot be rationally doubted. Descartes’ cogito (“I think, therefore I am”) is the standard example. If infallibilism is plausible, this must be the version it means.

Ernest Sosa describes the “classical foundationalism” that infallibilism belongs to:

“Classical foundationalism in epistemology is the view that: (i) every infallible, indubitable belief is justified, (ii) every belief deductively inferred from justified beliefs is itself justified, and (iii) every belief that is justified is so in virtue of (i) or (ii) above.”

Ernest Sosa, ‘The Raft and the Pyramid’ (1980)

Sosa pictures this as a pyramid: knowledge rests on a solid base of infallible beliefs, and everything else is built on top by valid reasoning. He contrasts it with the coherentist raft:

“Contemporary epistemology must choose between the solid security of the ancient foundationalist pyramid and the risky adventure of the new coherentist raft.”

Ernest Sosa, ‘The Raft and the Pyramid’ (1980)
Strength 1: it defeats Gettier

Every Gettier case depends on fallible justification: Smith’s evidence could have led him to a false belief, and in fact did with (d). Gettier’s own first assumption is that justification is fallible. If knowledge requires justification that guarantees truth, there is no room for luck, and Gettier cases never get started.

Strength 2: it fits how we talk

There seems to be a deep link between knowing and not being able to be wrong. “I know it, but I might be mistaken” sounds odd. Infallibilism takes that link seriously.

Objection: scepticism

Very few beliefs cannot be rationally doubted without absurdity. The only propositions we could know would be the cogito and some a priori truths. We would lose almost all knowledge from perception, memory, testimony and science. The definition goes too far and leads to scepticism.

Response

The infallibilist may accept this. Perhaps we really do know much less than we assume, and most of what we call knowledge is in fact well-justified belief. A definition should be accurate, not comforting.

Counter-response

A definition of a concept is meant to capture how the concept is actually used. If a definition implies that nobody knows their own name or where they live, that tells against the definition rather than against our knowledge. A good definition should get the clear cases right.

C · Reliabilism

Reliabilism shifts attention from the reasons a person can give to the process that actually produced the belief. Its roots go back further than Gettier. According to Goldman and Beddor, Frank Ramsey (1931) wrote that a belief counts as knowledge if it is true, certain and obtained by a reliable process. David Armstrong (1973) offered an analysis of non-inferential knowledge that explicitly used the term “reliable”.

Reliabilist definition S knows that P if and only if:
  1. P is true;
  2. S believes that P; and
  3. S’s belief that P was produced by a reliable cognitive process.
Goldman’s central idea

“The justificational status of a belief is a function of the reliability of the process or processes that cause it, where (as a first approximation) reliability consists in the tendency of a process to produce beliefs that are true rather than false.”

Alvin Goldman, ‘What Is Justified Belief?’ (1979)

Goldman reaches this idea by asking what bad ways of forming beliefs have in common:

“Here are some examples: confused reasoning, wishful thinking, reliance on emotional attachment, mere hunch or guesswork, and hasty generalization. What do these faulty processes have in common? They share the feature of unreliability: they tend to produce error a large proportion of the time.”

Alvin Goldman, ‘What Is Justified Belief?’ (1979)

Sense perception

Seeing, hearing, touching: the most familiar reliable process.

Memory

Recalling what we have previously learnt or experienced.

Testimony

Believing what reliable others tell us.

Reliable processes

  • Sense perception
  • Memory
  • Testimony
  • Good reasoning
  • Introspection

Unreliable processes

  • Wishful thinking
  • Emotional attachment
  • Hunches and guesswork
  • Hasty generalisation
  • Confused reasoning

Example: I see a tree using normal vision, come to believe there is a tree in front of me, and there is. I know there is a tree, because my belief came from a reliable process. I do not need to be able to explain why vision is reliable, or even be aware that it is. The process only has to be reliable.

The course handout adds a helpful way to think about this: reliability is like a natural good, such as intelligence or strength. It benefits a creature, but it is not under our active control. We should not be praised or blamed for it, though we can be admired for it.

Strength 1: babies and animals

Reliabilism allows young children and animals to have knowledge. A toddler who sees their parent knows their parent is there, even though they could not give a justification. More intellectual definitions, which demand reasons, struggle to say this.

Strength 2: realistic standards

It is implausible that we need consciously available justification for every piece of knowledge, and implausible that knowledge needs absolute certainty. Reliabilism avoids both demands, and so avoids infallibilism’s slide into scepticism.

Strength 3: it explains justification

Goldman wanted an account that explains why some beliefs are justified, in terms that do not themselves presuppose epistemic ideas. Reliability is defined in terms of belief, truth and frequency, so it can do this explanatory work.

Objection 1: Henry in Barn County

Henry uses his normally reliable eyesight, believes there is a barn, and is looking at a real barn. All three reliabilist conditions seem to be met, yet he does not know. Zagzebski’s diagnosis, as the course handout explains it, is that a reliable process can come apart from truth: we can be right by accident rather than because the process worked. Until we can explain why the truth and the evidence are connected, we will be lost.

Response

Perception of barns is not reliable in Barn County. There, most “barn” beliefs formed from the road are false. If reliability is judged relative to the environment, Henry’s process is unreliable, and reliabilism correctly says he does not know.

Counter-response: the generality problem

This response only works if we describe Henry’s process narrowly (“seeing barns from this road”). Described broadly (“vision in daylight”), the process is highly reliable. Goldman himself identified this difficulty:

“A critical problem concerning our analysis is the degree of generality of the process-types in question. Input-output relations can be specified very broadly or very narrowly, and the degree of generality will partly determine the degree of reliability.”

Alvin Goldman, ‘What Is Justified Belief?’ (1979)

Without a principled way to choose the right description, “reliable” has no clear meaning, and the theory cannot give a definite verdict on Henry or anyone else.

Objection 2: Norman the clairvoyant

Laurence BonJour (1980) imagines Norman, who has a perfectly reliable power of clairvoyance but no evidence or reasons for or against having it. One day it produces the belief that the President is in New York City, with no experience attached, just the bare belief. The belief is true and reliably produced, so reliabilism says it is justified. Intuitively, says BonJour, Norman is not justified. Reliable but unreasoned belief does not seem good enough.

Response: approved-list reliabilism

Goldman later developed “two-stage” or “approved-list” reliabilism. People build up lists of processes they consider reliable (perception, memory) and unreliable (guesswork). Clairvoyance is not on our approved list, which explains why we judge Norman unjustified.

Objection 3: the benevolent demon

Goldman raises this problem against his own theory:

“Surely we can imagine a possible world in which wishful thinking is reliable. We can imagine a possible world where a benevolent demon so arranges things that beliefs formed by wishful thinking usually come true. This would make wishful thinking a reliable process in that possible world, but surely we don’t want to regard beliefs that result from wishful thinking as justified.”

Alvin Goldman, ‘What Is Justified Belief?’ (1979)
Goldman’s response

He suggests that what matters is a process’s success in “natural” situations, not situations involving manipulative demons, though he admits he is unsure:

“There are several possible ways to respond to this case and I am unsure which response is best.”

Alvin Goldman, ‘What Is Justified Belief?’ (1979)
Objection 4: the new evil demon

The reverse problem. Goldman and Beddor describe it:

“Imagine a world where an evil demon creates non-veridical perceptions of physical objects in everybody’s minds. All of these perceptions are qualitatively identical to ours, but are false in the world in question. Hence, their perceptual belief-forming processes (as judged by the facts in that world) are unreliable; and their beliefs so caused are unjustified. But since their perceptual experiences—hence evidence—are qualitatively identical to ours, shouldn’t those beliefs in the demon world be justified?”

Goldman and Beddor, ‘Reliabilist Epistemology’, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (2021)

The victims are doing everything right, so it seems wrong to call their beliefs unjustified. Reliabilism appears to judge them by their luck, not their rational conduct.

D · Virtue epistemology

Virtue epistemology is a development of reliabilism, associated with Ernest Sosa and Linda Zagzebski. It treats knowledge as a cognitive achievement: a success that results from the activity of our intellectual virtues.

“Beliefs are a special case of performances, epistemic performances.”

Ernest Sosa, as quoted in the course handout

An intellectual virtue is a skill of the mind that enables you to achieve a specific end. Good memory lets you recall things easily; good eyesight and colour vision let you perceive accurately (Sosa’s own standard examples); creativity makes it easier to produce new ideas. Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin used their intellectual virtues to reach their scientific discoveries. These are achievements that can be credited to them, which means we can be praised for knowledge and blamed for ignorance.

Already in ‘The Raft and the Pyramid’, Sosa pointed towards this idea. He suggested that justification belongs first to stable dispositions, and only then to particular beliefs:

“Secondary justification would then attach to particular beliefs in virtue of their source in intellectual virtues or other such justified dispositions.”

Ernest Sosa, ‘The Raft and the Pyramid’ (1980)

“In epistemology, there is reason to think that the most useful and illuminating notion of intellectual virtue will prove broader than our tradition would suggest and must give due weight not only to the subject and his intrinsic nature but also to his environment and to his epistemic community.”

Ernest Sosa, ‘The Raft and the Pyramid’ (1980)
Sosa’s archer: the three As
The three AsFor an archerFor a belief
AccuracyDid the arrow hit the target?Is the belief true?
AdroitnessWas the shot skilful and competent?Does it manifest epistemic virtue or competence?
AptnessDid it hit because it was skilful?Is it true because it is competent?

“Belief amounts to knowledge when apt: that is to say, when its correctness is attributable to a competence exercised in appropriate conditions.”

Ernest Sosa, as quoted in the course handout
Virtue epistemology definition (Sosa) S knows that P if and only if S aptly believes P: S’s belief is correct because of the exercise of an epistemic competence.
Strength 1: it explains Gettier

In Gettier cases the belief is true because of luck or coincidence, not intellectual virtue. Smith reasons well (his belief is adroit) and his belief is true (accurate), but it is true because of the coins in his own pocket, not because of his competence. It is not apt, so it is not knowledge. Goldman and Beddor describe how Sosa applies this to a similar case:

“Sosa claims that while S holds this belief because of the exercise of an epistemic competence, S’s belief isn’t correct because of the exercise of an epistemic competence.”

Goldman and Beddor, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (2021)
Strength 2: knowledge as achievement

It explains why we value knowledge more than lucky true belief, and why we praise people for knowing and criticise them for ignorance. Knowledge is credited to the knower in the way a winning shot is credited to the archer.

Strength 3: it keeps reliabilism’s advantages

Competences such as good eyesight are also reliable processes, so virtue epistemology still allows children and animals to know, and still avoids infallibilism’s demand for certainty.

Objection: Henry in Barn County again

The course handout argues that virtue epistemology solves Henry: his belief is accurate and adroit, but correct because of luck, so not apt. However, Goldman and Beddor report that the barn case has been thought to cause “particular trouble” for virtue epistemology:

“Henry forms a true belief that there’s a barn in front of him; what’s more, the fact that he correctly believes there’s a barn in front of him seems to be causally explained by an exercise of his visual competence.”

Goldman and Beddor, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (2021), citing Lackey (2007)

Henry is looking at a real barn, and his good eyesight is why he gets it right. So his belief seems to be true because of his competence, and therefore apt. Yet he does not know.

Response 1: “appropriate conditions”

Sosa’s definition requires competence “exercised in appropriate conditions”. Barn County, full of deliberate fakes, is not an appropriate environment for barn-spotting. Sosa himself said that intellectual virtue must give due weight to the subject’s environment. So Henry’s belief is not apt in the full sense, and he does not know.

Response 2: add safety (Pritchard)

Duncan Pritchard combines virtue epistemology with a “safety” requirement: a belief must be one that could not easily have been held falsely. Henry could very easily have been looking at a fake, so his belief is unsafe and not knowledge.

Counter-response

Both responses add something beyond virtue. Response 1 needs an account of “appropriate conditions” that does not simply mean “conditions in which you get knowledge”, or the definition becomes circular. Response 2 admits that virtue alone cannot handle every Gettier case. Goldman and Beddor conclude that whether such replies are adequate “is a matter of debate”.

Going further: epistemic vices (Quassim Cassam)

If intellectual virtues explain knowledge, intellectual vices may explain ignorance. Quassim Cassam defines them:

“An epistemic vice is blameworthy or otherwise reprehensible character trait, attitude, or way of thinking that systematically obstructs the gaining, keeping, or sharing of knowledge.”

Quassim Cassam, as quoted in the course handout

Signs of the vice of closed-mindedness include: reluctance to consider new information once a view has been “frozen upon”; denying or reinterpreting information that conflicts with your view; placing a particular premium on clarity, order and coherence; poor appreciation of other perspectives; very high self-confidence; and intolerance of those who disagree.

Weighing them up

TheoryGettier’s casesHenry in Barn CountyBiggest problem
JTB✗ Fails✗ FailsNot sufficient: justification is fallible
No false lemmas✓ Solves✗ FailsHenry infers nothing false; a fifth condition is unachievable
Infallibilism✓ Solves✓ SolvesLeads to scepticism
ReliabilismArguablyOnly if reliability depends on the environmentGenerality problem; Norman; demon cases
Virtue epistemology✓ SolvesDisputedDefining “appropriate conditions” without circularity

Remember Williamson’s alternative (Part 3): if every attempt keeps meeting new counter-examples, perhaps knowledge is basic and cannot be defined at all.

Reference

Glossary of technical terms

Search or browse the key vocabulary for this topic.

Ability knowledgeKnowing how to do something, e.g. ride a bicycle.
Acquaintance knowledgeKnowing a person, place or thing through direct contact, e.g. “I know John.”
Accuracy(Sosa) Whether a performance hits its target; for a belief, whether it is true.
Adroitness(Sosa) Whether a performance, or a belief, shows skill or competence.
Aptness(Sosa) Whether a performance is accurate because it is adroit. Apt belief is knowledge.
A prioriKnowable without relying on sense experience.
Approved-list reliabilismGoldman’s later view: we judge beliefs justified if they come from processes on our list of reliable ones.
Barn County (Henry)Goldman’s 1976 case: a justified true belief, not inferred from anything false, that is true by luck.
Benevolent demonGoldman’s case in which wishful thinking is made reliable, yet its beliefs still seem unjustified.
CertaintyFor infallibilism, a belief that cannot be rationally doubted, not merely a feeling of being sure.
Classical foundationalism(Sosa) The view that infallible, indubitable beliefs are justified, and everything else is justified by deduction from them.
Closure (principle of)If S is justified in believing P, and P entails Q, and S deduces Q from P, then S is justified in believing Q.
CogitoDescartes’ “I think, therefore I am”: a belief that cannot be rationally doubted.
Counter-exampleA case that shows a general claim or definition to be false.
EntailmentP entails Q if, whenever P is true, Q must also be true.
Epistemic competenceA disposition to arrive at the truth, such as good eyesight or memory.
Epistemic vice(Cassam) A trait or way of thinking that systematically obstructs gaining, keeping or sharing knowledge.
EpistemologyThe branch of philosophy concerned with knowledge.
Factive mental state(Williamson) A mental state you can only be in if its content is true, such as knowing.
FallibleCapable of being wrong.
Generality problemThe difficulty of deciding how broadly or narrowly to describe a belief-forming process, which changes how reliable it counts as.
Gettier caseA case of justified true belief that is not knowledge, usually because it is true by luck.
Iff“If and only if”: signals necessary and sufficient conditions.
Individually necessaryEach condition on its own is required.
InfallibilismThe view that knowledge requires justification that guarantees truth, i.e. certainty.
Intellectual virtueA skill or excellence of the mind that helps us reach truth.
Jointly sufficientAll the conditions together are enough.
JustificationReasons or evidence that support a belief.
LemmaA proposition used as a step in an argument towards a conclusion.
Necessary conditionA condition that must be met for something to be the case.
New evil demon problemPeople deceived by a demon have the same evidence as us, so their beliefs seem justified even though their processes are unreliable.
No false lemmasThe view that knowledge is justified true belief not inferred from anything false.
PropositionA claim that can be true or false.
Propositional knowledgeKnowing that something is the case.
Reliable processA belief-forming process that tends to produce beliefs that are true rather than false.
ReliabilismThe view that knowledge is true belief produced by a reliable cognitive process.
SafetyThe requirement that a belief could not easily have been held falsely.
ScepticismThe view that we have little or no knowledge.
Sufficient conditionA condition that, if met, guarantees that something is the case.
Tripartite view (JTB)Knowledge is justified true belief: three individually necessary and jointly sufficient conditions.
Virtue epistemologyThe view that knowledge is belief that is true because of the exercise of intellectual virtue.

Practice

Exam questions

Questions labelled with a series appeared in real AQA papers. The rest are A-level-style practice questions. Open each one for planning points.

3-mark questions

What is meant by a “necessary condition”? 3 marks

A-level style

Planning points
  • A condition that must be met for something to be the case.
  • Without it, you cannot have the thing.
  • Example: being a mammal is necessary for being a dog.

What is propositional knowledge? 3 marks

A-level style

Planning points
  • Knowing that something is the case.
  • Its content is a proposition that can be true or false.
  • Example; contrast with ability or acquaintance knowledge.

What is a “false lemma”? 3 marks

A-level style

Planning points
  • A lemma is a proposition used as a step in reasoning towards a conclusion.
  • A false lemma is such a step that is untrue.
  • Example: “Jones will get the job” in Gettier’s Case I.

5-mark questions

Explain the tripartite view of propositional knowledge. 5 marks

AQA, June 2025

Planning points
  • S knows that P iff P is true, S believes that P, and S is justified in believing that P.
  • Explain what each condition requires and why it seems needed.
  • The conditions are individually necessary and jointly sufficient.

Explain the reliabilist definition of knowledge. 5 marks

AQA, June 2022

Planning points
  • Knowledge is true belief produced by a reliable cognitive process.
  • A reliable process tends to produce beliefs that are true rather than false (Goldman); examples.
  • The subject need not be aware of the process or its reliability, so infants and animals can know.

Explain how the “Henry in Barn County” example challenges the no false lemmas definition of knowledge. 5 marks

A-level style

Planning points
  • State the four conditions of the no false lemmas definition.
  • Henry has a justified true belief that he sees a barn.
  • The belief is perceptual, not inferred from anything false, so all four conditions are met.
  • But it is true by luck, so intuitively he does not know: the definition is not sufficient.

Explain why infallibilism might lead to scepticism. 5 marks

A-level style

Planning points
  • Infallibilism requires certainty: beliefs that cannot be rationally doubted.
  • Very few beliefs meet this standard: the cogito and some a priori truths.
  • Perception, memory, testimony and science are all fallible, so most ordinary beliefs would not count as knowledge.

12-mark questions

Explain one of Gettier’s original counter-examples and explain how the addition of a “no false lemmas” condition responds to it. 12 marks

AQA, June 2023

Planning points
  • The tripartite definition, and Gettier’s aim: to show the conditions are not jointly sufficient.
  • Gettier’s two assumptions: justification is fallible; justification carries over through deduction.
  • Case I in full: evidence → (d) → (e); the twist; JTB is met but Smith does not know.
  • The false lemma: “Jones will get the job”.
  • The fourth condition, and how it means Smith does not know.

Explain how an account of epistemic virtue can be used to show why Smith lacks knowledge in one of Gettier’s original counter-examples. 12 marks

AQA, November 2021

Planning points
  • Outline one of Gettier’s original cases.
  • Virtue epistemology: knowledge as cognitive achievement; intellectual virtues.
  • Sosa’s archer: accuracy, adroitness, aptness.
  • Smith’s belief is accurate and adroit, but true because of luck, not competence.
  • So it is not apt, and not knowledge.

Explain reliabilism and explain how the generality problem challenges it. 12 marks

A-level style

Planning points
  • The reliabilist definition; Goldman on reliability as a tendency to produce true beliefs.
  • Examples of reliable and unreliable processes.
  • The generality problem: processes can be described broadly or narrowly, which changes their reliability.
  • Apply to Henry: “vision” (reliable) versus “seeing barns from this road” (unreliable).

25-mark questions

How should propositional knowledge be defined? 25 marks

AQA, specimen paper

Planning points
  • State your thesis at the start (e.g. virtue epistemology gives the best definition).
  • JTB, and Gettier’s challenge to its sufficiency.
  • No false lemmas and Henry; infallibilism and scepticism; reliabilism and the generality problem.
  • Virtue epistemology: its handling of Gettier; Henry as an objection; the “appropriate conditions” response.
  • Alternative conclusion: Williamson, knowledge cannot be defined.

Is knowledge justified true belief? 25 marks

A-level style

Planning points
  • Thesis → JTB explained → challenges to each condition being necessary, with responses → Gettier attacks sufficiency → evaluate whether any amended version survives → conclusion.

Does reliabilism give a satisfactory definition of knowledge? 25 marks

A-level style

Planning points
  • Thesis → reliabilism explained → strengths (infants and animals, avoids certainty) → Henry, with the environment response → generality problem → Norman → demon cases → conclusion (e.g. virtue epistemology keeps the strengths and better explains luck).
Structuring a 25-mark answer

1. Thesis in your first sentence. 2. Each paragraph: point → objection → response → mini-judgement linked to your thesis. 3. A conclusion that follows from your arguments, with no new material.
